# Deployment Topologies and Reliability {#sec-deployment}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**Chapter status: drafted.** One small measurement, about a minute of compute:
72 short calls — three tasks × three sampling conditions × eight retries —
asking a model to emit the same tool call repeatedly, to find out whether
retrying an agent step reproduces it. Everything else here is ordinary
distributed-systems practice applied to a non-deterministic caller, and is cited
rather than re-derived. Software: `ollama` 0.24.0 serving `llama3.2:3b`, Python
3.14.5, Apple Silicon.
:::

**Learning objectives.** After this chapter you can:

- choose between a managed agent runtime and your own containers with a stated
  rationale rather than a preference;
- decide where a conversation lives, and what that decision costs you when you
  scale out;
- run agents that outlive a request, with progress and cancellation;
- say what durable execution demands of your tool code before you adopt it;
- make a side-effecting step safe to retry, and derive the idempotency key from
  the right place;
- write the compensating action for each tool, and identify the one that has
  none;
- bound a session by steps, tokens and wall-clock time;
- ship a change to an agent behind a canary, with a rollback trigger agreed in
  advance.

## Where the agent actually runs {#sec-deployment-where}

The first decision is a boring one, and teams routinely make it by habit. There
are three shapes, and the honest way to choose is to name which constraint is
binding.

| | you get | you give up | choose it when |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| **Managed agent runtime** | session state, retries, scaling and traces without writing them | control over the loop, the ability to run in your own network, and portability | speed to ship matters more than control, and no data-residency rule blocks it |
| **Your own containers** | full control of the loop, the network and the data path | building session storage, cancellation, retry semantics and observability yourself | residency or an existing platform makes it necessary — not because it feels more serious |
| **Serverless functions** | scale-to-zero and no idle cost | long runs, because execution is time-boxed | traffic is spiky and every task finishes in seconds |

: Three shapes, and the constraint that should pick one
{tbl-colwidths="[20,28,28,24]"}

[The third is the one that surprises teams.]{.hl} An agent loop is not a
request handler: it can take minutes, and a platform that caps execution at a
few seconds will kill it in the middle, after the tools have already run. If
your runtime has a hard execution ceiling, the loop has to move behind a queue —
which is @sec-deployment-long, and is a change to the product, not to the
deployment.

## Where the conversation lives {#sec-deployment-state}

An agent is a loop over messages, so the messages have to be somewhere. Three
places, in increasing order of what they let you do:

**In the process.** Simple, fast, and it means one instance owns a session
forever. Any restart, deploy or scale-in loses conversations, and load balancing
has to pin a user to an instance — which is the constraint that eventually
forces the change.

**In a session store.** The loop reads the history at the start of a turn and
writes it back at the end. Any instance can serve any turn, restarts are
survivable, and the store's latency is now on every turn. This is the default
that fits almost everything.

**In the client.** The caller sends the whole history each turn. The server is
genuinely stateless and trivially scalable. The price is a request that grows
on the wire every turn, and a client that can edit the history, which
@sec-agent-security has opinions about. The token bill is the same for all
three options (see the margin note).

::: {.column-margin}
The token cost of carrying a history is easy to underestimate, and it is not
specific to *where* the history lives. A twenty-turn conversation resends
nineteen turns on the last request, so the last prompt grows linearly and the
session's total prompt tokens grow roughly quadratically — the same arithmetic
whether the client sent the history or a server-side session store did, because
what you pay for is what reaches the model. What client-held state changes is
who can edit it, not what it costs — and @sec-serving's
measurements show prefill dominating latency well before that becomes a bill
problem. Prompt caching helps exactly here, provided the history is append-only
and nothing volatile sits at the top.
:::

## Agents that outlive a request {#sec-deployment-long}

Once a task takes minutes, holding an HTTP connection open for it stops being
reasonable: clients time out, load balancers cut idle connections, and a deploy
kills whatever was in flight.

The shape that works is the one every long-running system converges on. Accept
the request, write a job, return an id. A worker picks the job up. The client
polls or subscribes for progress. Three things that are easy to skip and painful
to add later:

- **Progress that means something.** "Step 4 of an unknown number" is not
  progress. Emit the step, the tool just called, and tokens spent so far —
  @sec-observability is where those become traces.
- **Cancellation that actually stops work.** A cancel flag the loop never checks
  is decoration. The loop must read it between steps, and the tools must be
  cancellable or at least idempotent, because a cancel arriving mid-tool-call
  cannot undo what the tool has already started.
- **A dead-letter path.** Jobs that fail repeatedly must land somewhere a human
  sees, rather than being retried forever — the same problem as
  @sec-deployment-retry, in a different form.

## Durable execution, and what replay demands of your code {#sec-deployment-durable}

If a worker crashes halfway through a twelve-step agent run, what happens? The
naive answer — start again — re-executes every tool call, including the ones
that already sent something.

**Durable execution** engines answer this by recording each completed step and
replaying the history after a crash, so completed work is not repeated. Temporal
and Restate are the usual examples, and the idea long predates agents.

One caveat decides how much this buys you. A step counts as completed only once
its result is recorded, so a step that was *running* when the worker died is run
again. If the tool acted and the worker crashed before the engine recorded the
result, the effect happens twice. Temporal's documentation says this directly:
an activity is recorded as completed once but may be executed more than once.
Durable execution removes the re-running of finished steps; it does not remove
the need for idempotent tools (@sec-deployment-idempotency).

The part that matters for adopting one is not the engine, it is the contract it
imposes on your code:

[Replay means your workflow function runs again from the top, and every
completed step returns its recorded result instead of executing.]{.hl} For that
to be sound, the function has to be *deterministic*: same history, same
sequence of decisions. Reading the clock, generating a random id or calling an
API directly from workflow code all break it, because the replay would take a
different path than the original.

This is awkward for agents, and it is worth being blunt about it. **An LLM
call has to be treated as an external, potentially non-deterministic operation**
— even at temperature 0, where batching, hardware and a silent model update all
move the output. The resolution is
structural rather than clever: the model call is a *step* — an activity, in
Temporal's vocabulary — whose result is recorded and replayed, not a decision
made inside workflow code. The workflow orchestrates; the non-determinism lives
in the steps it records.

That is a real constraint on tool design (@sec-tool-design), and adopting a
durable engine after the fact usually means rewriting the loop rather than
wrapping it.

## Retrying a step is not retrying a request {#sec-deployment-retry}

@sec-gateway dealt with retries against a *provider*: the failure there is
amplification, and the fix is backoff, jitter, circuit breakers and a retry
budget. This section is about retrying an *agent step*, where the failure is
different and worse.

A provider retry that succeeds twice costs you money. An agent-step retry that
succeeds twice sends the email twice.

The interesting question underneath is one people assume rather than measure:
**when you retry the step, do you get the same tool call?** The measurement:
a model was asked to emit one `send_email` call, eight times, for each of three
tasks under three sampling conditions. The three tasks leave the model
progressively more to decide: `clear` names the recipient, `vague` is loosely
worded, and `choice` (quoted below) leaves the recipient to the model. In the
`seed` column, `0` is a fixed seed and `None` means no seed was set.
`identical` is byte equality of the whole tool-call payload (the tool name and
all its arguments) across all eight retries; `distinct to` and `distinct subj`
count unique values of the recipient and subject arguments only.

```text
    task  temp   seed  identical  distinct to  distinct subj
   clear   0.0      0       True            1              1
   clear   0.0   None       True            1              1
   clear   0.7   None      False            1              1
   vague   0.0      0       True            1              1
   vague   0.0   None       True            1              1
   vague   0.7   None      False            1              6
  choice   0.0      0       True            1              1
  choice   0.0   None       True            1              1
  choice   0.7   None      False            5              2
```

Read the last row. The task was *"the pump failed, notify whoever needs to
know"*, and across eight retries at temperature 0.7 the model chose **five
different recipients**:

```text
  3x  maintenance@factory.com
  2x  maintenance@company.com
  1x  pump_repair_team@example.com
  1x  maintenance-team@company.com
  1x  engineering@company.com
```

[A retry did not repeat the action. It performed a different one.]{.hl} Every
address is invented, and a retry loop with no idempotency protection would have
mailed several of them.

**Read five as a floor, not an estimate.** Eight draws cannot bound how many
addresses the model is willing to invent. Ecologists face the same problem when
counting species, and their Chao1 estimator uses the values seen exactly once
($f_1$) and exactly twice ($f_2$) to estimate how many were never seen. With
this distribution — one address three times, one twice, three once each, so
$f_1 = 3$ and $f_2 = 1$ — the classic form $5 + f_1^2/(2f_2)$ gives **9.5**, and
the small-sample bias-corrected form
$5 + \frac{n-1}{n}\cdot\frac{f_1(f_1-1)}{2(f_2+1)}$ gives about 6.3 with $n = 8$ draws.
Eight draws are far too few to choose between them, but both are above five,
because three singletons in eight draws is the signature of a long tail you
have not sampled. In the other direction,
eight identical outputs at temperature 0 give a Wilson 95% interval of about
**[68%, 100%]** on the repeat rate, so "byte-identical eight times" is
compatible with a true repeat rate near two thirds. Neither correction changes
the design conclusion. Both change what may be claimed: this establishes that
the failure exists and reproduces easily, not how often it happens on your
endpoint.

Three things this does *not* say, all of which matter.

**Temperature 0 is not the fix, it is a different risk.** At temperature 0 all
eight retries were byte-identical for every task — including `choice`, which
deterministically invented `maintenance@company.com`. Reproducible and still
wrong. Determinism makes a retry *repeatable*; it does not make the underlying
decision correct.

**And a condition this table is missing settles a related question.**
@sec-prompting ran the same check at larger scale and found that a **fixed seed
at temperature 0.7** also produced identical output on all 30 documents across
ten repeats. So the axis here is not really temperature; it is whether the
sampler is pinned. That is worth knowing before you reach for temperature 0 as
a reliability lever, because it costs you diversity you may want and buys you
something a seed buys more cheaply — on a server that supports a seed and batches
your request the same way each time. Many hosted APIs offer no seed, or only a
best-effort one, for the reason in the next paragraph.

**And this determinism is a property of a single-stream local server, not a
guarantee.** The load-bearing condition is **batch invariance**: the reduction
kernels behind matmul, normalisation and attention take different code paths at
different batch sizes, so the same prompt in a batch of one and a batch of
seventeen can decode differently even at temperature 0
[@he2025nondeterminism]. Hosted APIs batch your request with strangers. Treat
temperature 0 as a variance reduction, never as an idempotency mechanism.

::: {.column-margin}
The pattern in the table is worth more than the individual numbers, and it is
finer than "temperature is the problem". At 0.7 *no* task was byte-identical —
including `clear`, which named the recipient and still varied in the body. What
ambiguity changed is *which field* moved: `clear` kept the recipient and the
subject, `vague` produced six subject lines, `choice` produced five recipients.
Temperature perturbs everything; the task decides whether the perturbation
lands on a field that has a side effect. This is also why a key derived from
*any* part of the payload is unsafe, not only one built from the recipient:
which field moves depends on the task.
:::

## Idempotency keys, and where the key comes from {#sec-deployment-idempotency}

The standard fix for a duplicated side effect is an **idempotency key**: the
caller supplies a key, the receiver records it, and a second request carrying a
key it has already seen returns the first result instead of acting again.

The measurement above settles the design question that usually gets hand-waved:

[The key cannot be derived from the model's output.]{.hl} Hashing the tool
arguments seems natural and fails exactly when you need it: the `choice` retries
produced five different argument sets, so five different hashes, so five emails.
A key computed from a non-deterministic value is not a key.

So derive it from something upstream and stable:

| key derived from | dedupes a retry? | notes |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Hash of tool arguments | [no]{.con} | changes when the model changes its mind — the failure this section measured |
| Random id per attempt | [no]{.con} | a new key every retry, which is the same as having none. A random id generated *once* per operation and stored before the first attempt is fine — that is what Stripe suggests; the mistake is generating it per attempt |
| `(session id, step index)` | [yes]{.pro} | stable across retries of the same step — add a sub-call index when one step makes several side-effecting calls, or they collide |
| Upstream request id | [yes]{.pro} | right when one request must produce at most one side effect end to end |

: Four candidate keys, and the two that work {tbl-colwidths="[26,18,56]"}

The step index is stable only if it comes from a history that survived the
crash — a session store or a durable engine's record. If a restart runs the
agent from scratch, the model may make the same call at a different step, and
the key changes with it.

Scope the key to the tenant as well, so two customers cannot collide on the same
logical operation id.

Three implementation notes decide whether it works in practice.

**Decide what happens when the key repeats with different arguments.** The
tempting behaviour — return the stored result — is wrong: it silently answers a
*different* request with an old answer. Stripe's API stores a fingerprint of the
request alongside the key and rejects a reuse whose parameters do not match, and
that is the behaviour to copy. Store the arguments with the record, compare on
replay, and fail loudly on a mismatch.

**The record and the effect must commit together.** When the effect is a row in
your own database that is one transaction and the problem is solved. When the
effect is a remote call — which is the case for every interesting tool,
including the `send_email` this chapter keeps using — it is not, because an
HTTP request cannot join your transaction. This is the dual-write problem, and
the standard answer is the **transactional outbox**: in one transaction, write
the idempotency record *and* a row describing the intended call; a separate
publisher reads the outbox and performs the call *at least once* — it may
repeat the call after a crash, but it never skips it — carrying the key so the
receiver dedupes it. You have not removed the duplicate. You have moved it
somewhere a key can absorb it.

That last step assumes the receiver honours idempotency keys. Payment APIs such
as Stripe's do; plain SMTP does not, and many email and messaging APIs do not
either. Against such a receiver, at-least-once means "occasionally twice". What
remains is to make the window small — record "sending" before the call, and
after a crash check the provider's own log before sending again — and to know
that the window exists.

**The retention window must outlast your longest retry.** Easy to set to five
minutes and then discover was needed for six hours, because the queue was
backed up and the job was redelivered the next morning.

## Compensation: there is no rollback for a sent email {#sec-deployment-compensation}

Idempotency stops an action happening twice. It does nothing about an action
that should not have happened once.

Databases give you transactions. The tools an agent calls mostly do not, so the
pattern is a **compensating action**: for each side effect, the operation that
undoes it — and the discipline is to write that column before shipping the tool,
not after the incident.

| tool | compensation | honest? |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Create a record | delete it | [mostly]{.pro} — the row goes, but anything that already fired on its creation (a webhook, a downstream event, a sent notification) does not un-fire |
| Charge a card | refund | mostly — the fee and the statement line survive |
| Book a slot | cancel | usually — but anyone turned away while the slot was held stays turned away |
| Post to a channel | delete the message | [no — people read it]{.con} |
| Send an email | [nothing]{.con} | [no]{.con} |

: Compensations, and the two rows with no real undo
{tbl-colwidths="[24,30,46]"}

[The bottom two rows are the design constraint.]{.hl} When a tool has no
compensation, the control has to move *earlier* — an approval gate before the
action rather than an undo after it, which is @sec-guardrails' subject. That is
a product decision disguised as an engineering one, and the compensation table
is what forces somebody to make it deliberately.

A useful habit when writing tools (@sec-tool-design): give every side-effecting
tool a dry-run mode. It makes the compensation table testable and it gives the
agent a way to check its own plan before committing to it.

## Three ceilings every agent needs {#sec-deployment-ceilings}

@sec-agent-anatomy measured why they are needed: with one protocol, sixty
percent of the easiest tasks never stopped on their own and ran until the step
cap — although each run already had the answer at step 0 — so an accuracy column
that looked like a reasoning result was really a termination result. Three
limits, and they catch different failures:

| ceiling | catches | what to do at the limit |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Steps** | the loop that keeps calling tools | stop, return partial work, mark it unfinished |
| **Tokens** | the run that stays cheap per step and expensive overall | stop and report spend — @sec-gateway enforces a related budget per virtual key |
| **Wall clock** | the tool that hangs, which neither other limit sees | cancel, and make sure cancellation reaches the tool |

: Three ceilings, three different failures {tbl-colwidths="[16,42,42]"}

All three are needed because each is blind to the others' failure. A step cap
does not stop one tool hanging for an hour; a wall-clock timeout does not stop
sixty fast steps burning a budget; a token cap does not stop a loop that reads
the same small file forever.

And hitting a ceiling is a **result**, not an error to swallow. It must appear
in the response, in the trace, and in your evaluation as a distinct outcome —
@sec-agent-eval's termination rate is exactly this number, and an agent that
looks 85% accurate while hitting its cap on a third of runs is not an 85%
accurate agent.

## Shipping a change: versions, canaries and rollback {#sec-deployment-release}

Everything so far is about surviving a failure while a run is in progress. The
other common way an agent breaks in production is a deploy: a new prompt, a new
model version, a reworded tool description. Four habits make a deploy
survivable.

**Version the whole behaviour, not only the code.** What an agent does is set by
its code, its prompts, the pinned model version (@sec-gateway-versions), the tool
definitions, and settings such as temperature and the three ceilings. Release
them together, under one release id, and record that id on every trace
(@sec-observability). A prompt edited in a dashboard without a new release id is
a deploy that nobody can attribute or roll back — and the "step change that
lines up with a release" that @sec-production-eval diagnoses is visible only if
the release was recorded.

**Roll out to a slice first.** A **canary** sends a small share of live
traffic — say 5% — to the new release, and compares it with the old release on
the same traffic: error rate, latency, cost per run, the share of runs that hit
a ceiling, and whatever quality signal you have. The share grows in stages
(5% → 25% → 100%) only while the canary is not worse, and traffic moves back
automatically when a threshold is crossed. A **shadow** deployment — the new
release runs on a copy of live inputs, but nobody is shown its output — is safe
for a chatbot and dangerous for an agent, because a shadow agent with real
tools sends real emails. Its side-effecting tools must run in dry-run mode
(@sec-deployment-compensation). What each of these rungs can and cannot detect
is @sec-production-eval's subject.

**Agree the rollback trigger before the deploy.** A **service level objective
(SLO)** is a target over a time window, measured by a *service level indicator
(SLI)* — for example, "99.5% of agent runs in a 30-day window finish without an
error or a ceiling". The 0.5% that may fail is the **error budget**: at 200,000
runs a month, 1,000 runs. A canary that burns that budget much faster than the
old release is rolled back by rule, not after an argument during an incident.
Choose the indicator with care: an HTTP 200 is not a successful run, because a
run can return 200 and still have hit a ceiling or given a wrong answer
(@sec-observability). Mind the size of the slice, too. A 5% canary on 200,000
runs a month sees about 330 runs a day, so at a 0.5% baseline it expects fewer
than two failures a day. That is enough to catch a release that breaks badly,
and far too few to notice one that is slightly worse. An A/B test run on the same
5% share has the same power problem: small effects need a larger share, a longer
run and a sample size worked out in advance.

**Rollback undoes the code, not the effects.** Rolling back restores the old
behaviour for *new* runs. It does not unsend the emails the bad release sent —
that is the compensation table — and it does not settle what happens to runs
that are still in flight. A durable workflow that started under the new code and
is replayed by the old code (or the reverse) can take a different path, which is
the determinism rule of @sec-deployment-durable again. Durable engines provide
workflow versioning for this (in Temporal's Python SDK, `workflow.patched()`);
the simple rule is to let every in-flight run finish on the version it started
with.

## Intuition checks {#sec-deployment-intuition}

Answer each one before you open it. Two of them turn on the retry measurement in
this chapter — what temperature 0 does and does not buy you, and why the
idempotency key cannot come from the model — and the rest are the questions
that decide whether a working prototype survives being deployed at all.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 1. Your agent runs fine locally and gets killed in production after 30 seconds.

You deployed a loop onto a request handler.

Serverless platforms cap execution time, many load balancers cut a connection
that stays idle too long, and an agent loop is not a request: it can take minutes, and the cap arrives mid-run — after some
tools have already executed. The symptom is a truncated run with real side
effects and no result.

If the work reliably finishes inside a bound you control, raising the timeout to
match is a legitimate fix and much cheaper. Past that, the fix is structural:
accept the request, enqueue a job, return an id, and let a worker run the loop. That change also gives you the
place to put progress, cancellation and a dead-letter path.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 2. Is temperature 0 enough to make a retry safe?

No, and it confuses two different properties.

Measured here, temperature 0 made eight retries byte-identical for every task —
including one where the model deterministically invented a recipient address.
Reproducible and wrong. Determinism makes a retry *repeatable*; it does not make
the decision correct, and it does nothing about the effect having already
happened.

It is also not a guarantee. Hosted APIs do not promise bit-identical output at
temperature 0, because batching and reduction order vary with what else is in
flight. Idempotency has to come from a key, not from sampling settings.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 3. Why not hash the tool arguments for the idempotency key?

Because the arguments are the model's output, and the model's output is exactly
what varies between retries.

Measured: for the task *"the pump failed, notify whoever needs to know"*, eight
retries at temperature 0.7 produced **five different recipient addresses**. Five
argument sets, five hashes, five emails — the key would have deduped nothing at
the moment it was needed.

Derive the key from something upstream and stable: `(session id, step index)`,
or the request id when one request must produce at most one effect.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 4. Which of your tools has no compensating action?

Usually the one that talks to a person.

Creating a record can be deleted; a charge can be refunded, allowing for the fee
and the statement line; a booking can be cancelled. But deleting a posted
message cannot undo the fact that people have *already* read it, and a sent email
cannot be undone at all.

That is why the compensation table has to be written before shipping rather than
after an incident. Where the compensation column says "none", the control moves
earlier — an approval gate before the action (@sec-guardrails) — and somebody
outside engineering has to agree to it.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 5. You added durable execution and your agent now behaves strangely on replay.

Something non-deterministic is running inside workflow code.

Replay re-runs the workflow function from the top, returning recorded results
for completed steps. That is only sound if the function takes the same path
every time, so reading the clock, generating a random id, or calling an API
directly from workflow code all break it.

For agents the specific trap is obvious once stated: the LLM call is the least
deterministic thing you have, so it must be a recorded *step*, not a decision
made in workflow code. The workflow orchestrates; the non-determinism lives in
the steps it records.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 6. A step cap is set. Do you still need a timeout?

Yes, because they are blind to each other.

A step cap does not stop one tool hanging for an hour — that is zero additional
steps. A wall-clock timeout does not stop sixty fast steps burning a budget. A
token cap does not stop a loop that reads the same small file forever.

Set all three, and treat hitting any of them as a distinct outcome that appears
in the response, the trace and the evaluation. @sec-agent-eval's termination
rate is that number, and an agent reported as 85% accurate while capping out on
a third of runs has not been measured honestly.
:::

## Interview questions {#sec-deployment-interview}

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**On sourcing — the same caveat as @sec-text-as-data.** The questions below
recur in the two credible open sources this book uses throughout, plus the ones
this chapter's own measurement makes answerable.
:::

### Testing whether you understand the failure

**Q: Your agent's worker crashes mid-run. What did it leave behind?**

Whatever the completed tool calls already did, with no record that they
completed. A naive restart re-executes them. Name the two answers: durable
execution, which records each step and replays the history so completed work is
not repeated; or idempotency keys on the side-effecting tools, so re-execution
is harmless. Most systems need the second regardless, because durable engines
run each step *at least once*: a crash after the tool acted but before the
engine recorded the result re-runs that step.

**Q: Is retrying an LLM step idempotent?**

Not by default, and not for the reason people expect. Beyond the effect having
already happened, the retry may not even repeat the same action — measured here,
a vague task produced five different recipient addresses across eight retries.
Temperature 0 made retries byte-identical on a local server, but that is a
variance reduction, not a guarantee, and hosted APIs do not promise it.

**Q: Where does an idempotency key come from?**

Somewhere upstream and stable — `(session id, step index)`, or the request id.
Explicitly *not* a hash of the tool arguments, because those are the model's
output and vary between retries. Then two details that decide whether it works:
the key must commit atomically with the effect — which for a remote call means
an outbox, since an HTTP request cannot join your transaction — and the
retention window must outlast your longest retry.

### Testing whether you have shipped one

**Q: Design deployment for an agent whose tasks take twenty minutes.**

Queue-backed, because a twenty-minute HTTP request does not survive a deploy or
a load balancer. Accept, enqueue, return an id; a worker runs the loop; the
client polls or subscribes. Then the three things that are painful to add later:
meaningful progress, cancellation the loop actually checks between steps, and a
dead-letter path so failures reach a human instead of retrying forever. Add the
three ceilings and make hitting one a reported outcome.

**Q: Where does the conversation live, and what does that cost?**

In the process is simplest and pins a user to an instance, so restarts lose
sessions. A session store is the default: any instance serves any turn, at the
cost of the store's latency on every turn. Client-held history makes the server
stateless but lets the client edit the history, which is a security question
(@sec-agent-security). None of the three changes the token bill: the model is sent
the whole conversation every turn wherever it is stored, so prompt tokens grow over
the session — @sec-serving's cost arithmetic.

**Q: An agent posted a wrong message to a customer channel. What is your review about?**

Not the model. Whether that tool had a compensation, whether the compensation is
real — deleting a message people already read is not an undo — and if it is not,
why the action was not behind an approval gate. Then whether it could have been
a duplicate rather than a decision, which is the idempotency question, and
whether the run hit a ceiling and was reported as a success.

**Q: How would you roll out a new prompt for an agent that sends emails?**

As a release: the prompt, the pinned model, the tool definitions and the
settings under one id recorded on every trace. Then a canary on a small slice,
compared with the old release on error rate, ceiling hits, cost and a quality
signal, with a rollback trigger taken from the SLO's error budget and agreed in
advance. Not a plain shadow deployment, because a shadow agent with a real
`send_email` sends real mail — shadow only with tools in dry-run mode. And say
what rollback cannot do: it does not unsend what the canary already sent.

## The 2026 toolbox {#sec-deployment-tools}

Almost nothing in this chapter needed a library — the measurement was 72 calls
to a local model, and everything else is a property of your own loop. The second
table is the one that matters, and it splits cleanly in two: durable execution
engines that impose the determinism contract described above, and plain task
queues that do not.

## Lab: make a step safe to retry {#sec-deployment-lab}

Take an agent with at least one side-effecting tool. If you do not have one, a
`send_email` that appends to a file is enough — the point is to *see* the
duplicate.

### Step 1 — reproduce the duplicate

Run the agent, kill the worker after the tool executes but before the result is
recorded, and restart. Count the effects. You should get two. If you cannot make
it happen on purpose, you cannot claim it will not happen by accident.

### Step 2 — measure your own retry determinism

Ask your model for the same tool call ten times at your production temperature.
Count distinct argument sets. Then repeat with one deliberately under-specified
task. The gap between those two numbers is how much your prompt is protecting
you.

### Step 3 — add an idempotency key from the right place

Key on `(session id, step index)`, not on the arguments. Repeat step 1. The
second execution must return the first result without acting.

### Step 4 — put the key and the effect in one transaction

A file append cannot join a database transaction, so for this step make the
fake `send_email` insert a row into the same database (SQLite is enough) that
holds the idempotency records, and write both in one transaction. For a real
remote call, use the outbox described above instead.
Then re-run step 1, killing the worker *between* the effect and the record.
If the duplicate comes back, the write was not atomic — which is the bug this
step exists to expose.

### Step 5 — write the compensation table

Every side-effecting tool, its compensating action, and an honest note on
whether the compensation is real. Circulate it. The rows with no compensation
are the ones that need an approval gate, and that is a conversation with
somebody outside engineering.

### Step 6 — set the three ceilings and trip each one

Steps, tokens, wall clock. Write a task that trips each ceiling separately —
a loop, an expensive run, a hanging tool — and confirm the agent stops, reports
which ceiling it hit, and that the outcome is distinguishable from success.

### What to hand in

The duplicate count before and after the key; your distinct-argument counts for
a clear and a vague task; the compensation table with its honest column; and
evidence that each of the three ceilings fires and is reported.

## Exercises {#sec-deployment-exercises}

1. **Force the duplicate.** Kill a worker between a tool executing and its
   result being recorded. Count the effects. Then add an idempotency key and
   show the count returns to one.

2. **Your determinism number.** Ask your production model for the same tool call
   ten times at your production temperature, and count distinct argument sets.
   Repeat with a deliberately vague instruction. Report both.

3. **The compensation table.** One row per side-effecting tool in a system you
   work on: the tool, its compensation, and whether the compensation is honest.
   Identify the rows that need an approval gate instead.

4. **Atomicity.** Find out whether your idempotency record commits together
   with the effect it guards. If the effect is a remote call it cannot, so
   implement the outbox instead and show that the duplicate is now absorbed by
   the receiver's key rather than prevented by your transaction. Either way,
   construct the interleaving that produces a duplicate and say how likely it
   is at your traffic.

5. **Trip all three ceilings.** Write three tasks that exhaust steps, tokens and
   wall clock respectively. Confirm each stops the agent, and that the three are
   distinguishable in your logs.

6. **The state decision, priced.** For a twenty-turn conversation, compute the
   total prompt tokens and use @sec-serving's arithmetic to turn them into
   latency and cost. That number is the same for client-held history and a
   session store, so price what does differ: the store's latency on every turn,
   what a deploy loses, and what a client that can edit its history can do.
   Then say which you would choose and why.

7. **Cancellation, honestly.** Send a cancel to a running agent and measure how
   long until work actually stops, and whether the in-flight tool call
   completed. If nothing checks the flag between steps, you do not have
   cancellation.

8. **Size the canary.** Write an SLO for an agent you know, with its SLI stated
   precisely, and compute the monthly error budget. Then compute how many runs a
   5% canary sees per day, and how many failures it should expect at your
   baseline failure rate. How much worse would a release have to be before a
   day of canary traffic could tell?

## Where to go deeper {#sec-deployment-deeper}

Before reading: pick the one tool in your system whose effect you would least
like to see happen twice, and find out today whether anything stops it. That
answer decides which of these you need first.

This chapter rests mostly on operational practice. The first table is the
operational literature and the engines that implement it, and nothing in it is a
research result; the second is the one research source the chapter cites.

| resource | what it is |
|:--|:--|
| [Making retries safe with idempotent APIs](https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/making-retries-safe-with-idempotent-APIs/) | the clearest write-up of the key, the record and the transaction boundary this chapter argues for |
| [Stripe's idempotent requests](https://docs.stripe.com/api/idempotent_requests) | the same design as a shipped public API, including the retention window most people set too short |
| [Handling Overload](https://sre.google/sre-book/handling-overload/) | the client-side retry budget, which stops the retries of failing jobs from turning into an outage |
| [Service Level Objectives](https://sre.google/sre-book/service-level-objectives/) | the Google SRE book's chapter on SLIs and SLOs; its error budget is the rollback trigger of @sec-deployment-release |
| [Temporal's workflow determinism rules](https://docs.temporal.io/workflow-definition) | the replay contract stated precisely; read this before adopting any durable engine, not after |
| [`temporalio/sdk-python`](https://github.com/temporalio/sdk-python) | the workflow/activity split in code, which is where the LLM call has to land |
| [`restate`](https://github.com/restatedev/restate) / [`dbos-transact-py`](https://github.com/dbos-inc/dbos-transact-py) | two lighter takes on durability, useful for seeing which parts of Temporal's contract are essential |
| [The saga pattern](https://microservices.io/patterns/data/saga.html) | compensation as a named pattern, with the failure modes the compensation table above only gestures at |
| [`celery`](https://github.com/celery/celery) / [`ray`](https://github.com/ray-project/ray) | the queue-backed shape without durability, when steps are already idempotent |

## What to remember {#sec-deployment-summary}

- **An agent loop is not a request handler.** It takes minutes, so a platform
  with an execution ceiling will kill it mid-run, after some tools have already
  fired. Once tasks outlive a request the shape is queue-backed: accept,
  enqueue, return an id, and add progress, cancellation and a dead-letter path
  while it is still cheap to add them.

- **Where the conversation lives is an operational and trust decision, not a
  token-cost one.** In-process pins a user to an instance and loses sessions on
  deploy. A session store is the default, with its latency on every turn. A
  client-held history makes the server stateless and lets the client edit it.
  Wherever it lives, the model receives the whole history each turn, so prompt
  tokens grow every turn — @sec-serving's arithmetic, and prefill dominates
  latency long before it dominates the bill.

- **Durable execution imposes determinism on your workflow code.** Replay re-runs
  the function and returns recorded results for completed steps, so clocks,
  random ids and direct API calls inside workflow code break it. The LLM call is
  the least deterministic thing you have, so it belongs in a recorded *step*,
  not in workflow code. Adopting an engine later usually means rewriting the
  loop. And a step that was running at the crash runs again, so the tools still
  need to be idempotent.

- **Retrying a step is not retrying a request.** @sec-gateway's retry problem is
  amplification; this one is duplication. And the retry may not even repeat the
  same action: asked to *notify whoever needs to know*, a model produced **five
  different recipient addresses across eight retries** at temperature 0.7.

- **Temperature 0 is variance reduction, not idempotency.** All eight retries
  were byte-identical at temperature 0 in this measurement — including the run
  that deterministically invented an address. Reproducible is not correct, and
  hosted APIs do not promise bit-identical output at temperature 0 anyway,
  because batching and reduction order vary with what else is in flight.

- **Derive the idempotency key from upstream, never from the model's output.**
  Hashing tool arguments fails exactly when it is needed — five argument sets
  means five hashes means five emails. Use `(session id, step index)` or the
  request id, commit the record together with the effect — via an outbox when
  the effect is a remote call, because an HTTP request cannot join your
  transaction — and give it a retention window longer than your longest retry.

- **Write the compensation table before shipping the tool.** A record can be
  deleted, a charge refunded, a booking cancelled. Deleting a posted message
  cannot undo its having been read, and a sent email cannot be undone at all.
  [Where the compensation column says "none", the control moves earlier]{.hl} —
  an approval gate rather than an undo — and that is a decision for somebody
  outside engineering.

- **Set all three ceilings, because each is blind to the others.** A step cap
  does not stop a hanging tool; a timeout does not stop sixty cheap steps
  burning a budget; a token cap does not stop a loop reading the same file
  forever. Hitting one is a *result*: it belongs in the response, the trace and
  the evaluation, and @sec-agent-eval's termination rate is where an agent that
  looks accurate while capping out gets caught.

- **Ship a change as one versioned release, to a slice first.** Code, prompts,
  pinned model, tool definitions and settings share one release id on every
  trace. A canary with a rollback trigger taken from the SLO's error budget
  catches a release that breaks badly; a shadow agent needs its tools in dry-run
  mode; and a rollback restores the code, not the effects the bad release
  already had.
